\begin{abstract}
The consistent-but-dangerous taxonomy flags a medical vision-language model (VLM) answer as \dang{} when it is
stable under paraphrase and unchanged when the image is removed. We ask whether this image-removal test can
rank models by how much they use the image. On a matched pair, MedGemma-4B and its general-purpose twin
Gemma-3-4B, we pose 3,365 questions over 907 CT, MRI, X-ray and pathology images under five probes, with
pre-registered endpoints and three probes registered before they were run. Image removal ranks MedGemma as the
less image-reliant model: its \dang{} share is 13.7 points higher\ci{10.0}{17.5}. All three probes that keep an
image in the input rank it as more reliant: MedGemma changes its answer more often when the image is swapped
(+5 points), blacked out (+20), or replaced by one on which the same question has the opposite answer (73\%
\vs 25\%, +48). Two confounds explain the reversal. Forced to answer yes or no without an image, Gemma-3 would
rather ask for the image on 29\% of questions, and its forced answers there are unrelated to its answers with
the image; allowed to say ``unknown'', both models decline on at least 93\%. And MedGemma's blind answers are
informative, so they match its image answers wherever image and prior agree: its excess \dang{} answers are all
correct. The \dang{} share also rests on a chance floor of 36--42\% on yes/no questions, and image reliance does
not flag wrong answers (AUROC 0.51). Image-removal results should be checked with in-format probes before they
are read as a model ignoring the image.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}
A model that answers a question about an image without using the image is not doing visual question
answering, however accurate it is. In general-domain VQA this concern produced balanced benchmarks and
prior-robust splits~\cite{goyal2017vqav2,agrawal2018dont}. Medical VQA is still mostly evaluated by accuracy,
where it matters more: a correct answer reached from language priors will be wrong on exactly the patients
whose images are unusual.

Accuracy cannot separate \emph{seeing} from \emph{guessing well}, and consistency under rephrasing cannot either:
a model that ignores the image is often \emph{more} consistent, because nothing visual perturbs
it~\cite{sadanandan2026psfmed}. Sadanandan and Behzadan~\cite{sadanandan2026consistent} therefore crossed the two
per sample. \emph{Consistent} means the answer is stable under paraphrase; \emph{image-reliant} means it changes
when the image is removed. This gives four quadrants: \textsc{Ideal} (consistent, reliant), \textsc{Fragile},
\dang{} (consistent but unchanged without the image) and \textsc{Worst}. On chest X-rays they found that
fine-tuning for consistency moves most answers into \dang{}.

A taxonomy like this invites comparisons between models, and a comparison is only as good as the probe
behind it. Removing the image changes the input format: a model asked about an image that is not there may
refuse, answer from priors, or guess, and none of these is the same as ignoring an image that is present. We
therefore ask whether image removal ranks two models the same way as probes that keep an image in the input. We
audit MedGemma-4B~\cite{sellergren2025medgemma}, a small open medical VLM, against Gemma-3-4B~\cite{gemma2025gemma3},
which has the same architecture and size but a general-purpose post-training, on CT, MRI, X-ray and pathology
questions from three public benchmarks. The design, endpoints and exclusions were frozen before the main run;
three further probes were registered after it and before they were run.

\Cref{fig:reversal} summarizes the answer. Image removal says MedGemma uses the image less than Gemma-3. A wrong
image, a black image and an image on which the same question has the opposite answer all say it uses the image
more. We trace the disagreement to two properties of image removal: it turns refusals into scored answers, and
it cannot distinguish a model that ignores the image from one whose prior agrees with it.

\centering

that uses the image should change its answer when the image changes. Only image removal, the probe that defines
the taxonomy, ranks Gemma-3 as the more image-reliant model.}
\label{fig:reversal}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Contributions.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
\item A side-by-side comparison of four reliance probes on the same questions and an architecture-matched model
pair, showing that image removal ranks the pair opposite to three in-format probes. Each probe has
precedent~\cite{sadanandan2026consistent,zafar2026see,lotfinia2026cxr}; to our knowledge their rankings of
models have not been compared.
\item Two confounds that explain the reversal, each with direct evidence: refusal under a forced yes/no format,
and agreement between a model's prior and the image.
\item Two corrections to the \dang{} share: its chance floor on yes/no questions (with Cohen's $\kappa$), and a
paired split into correct and wrong \dang{} answers.
\item A pre-registered, open pipeline across three datasets and four modalities, with a paraphrase set screened
pair by pair for equivalence and a finding that bf16 batching perturbs log-probabilities by up to 1~nat.
\end{itemize}

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}
\paragraph{Language priors in VQA.} Balanced pairs~\cite{goyal2017vqav2} and changing-prior
splits~\cite{agrawal2018dont} showed that general VQA models exploit answer priors; text-only baselines are the
medical analogue.

\paragraph{Does a medical VLM use the image?} PSF-Med~\cite{sadanandan2026psfmed} measured paraphrase flip rates
across medical VLMs on chest X-rays and noted that low flip rates often come with high text-only agreement. The
quadrant taxonomy~\cite{sadanandan2026consistent} defines reliance by image removal and corroborates it with a
KL-divergence score, a black image and random image swaps; on their models these checks agreed with image removal.
Zafar~\etal~\cite{zafar2026see} build blank, pixel-shuffled, absent and CLIP-retrieved hard-negative images to
define reliance metrics and train a model against them. Lotfinia~\etal~\cite{lotfinia2026cxr} swap and occlude
chest radiographs and find that model class (medical or general) does not predict image use; a question-only
medical model scores close to multimodal ones. Pathology VLMs reach high accuracy without the
image~\cite{zhang2026pathology}, and attention-based studies find that medical MLLMs often attend to irrelevant
regions~\cite{liu2026medmllmfail}. Grounding inputs can even hurt closed-ended accuracy~\cite{chen2026grounding};
HEAL-MedVQA~\cite{nguyen2025heal} and MedHEval~\cite{chang2025medheval} benchmark localization and
hallucination. These works use one probe or treat several as interchangeable; we compare the conclusions they
reach about the same pair of models.

\paragraph{Answering without the evidence.} MedVIGIL~\cite{jiang2026medvigil} tests whether models refuse when
visual evidence is broken, and Vohra~\cite{vohra2026hearsay} finds that frontier VLMs confabulate diagnoses for
images that were never attached. We find the converse for two small open models (they decline almost always when
allowed to) and show what this does to a reliance probe that forces an answer.

\paragraph{Selective prediction.} Ranking answers by a score and abstaining on the lowest is evaluated by AUROC
and risk--coverage~\cite{geifman2017selective}; we use it to ask whether reliance flags errors.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}
\subsection{Data}
\textbf{SLAKE}~\cite{liu2021slake} (English; CT, MRI, X-ray; 2,114 questions from test and validation, the
only dataset with modality labels; validation is added so each modality has 53--82 images).
\textbf{VQA-RAD}~\cite{lau2018vqarad} (radiology, clinician-written; all 451 test questions, from the
original release). \textbf{PathVQA}~\cite{he2020pathvqa} (pathology, generated from textbook captions; 600
yes/no and 200 open test questions sampled with a fixed seed). A question is yes/no if its gold answer is
\emph{yes} or \emph{no}. The \textbf{primary analysis set} is the 1,206 yes/no \emph{test} questions on 670
images. Sampling, partner images and image hashes are fixed in committed manifests (SHA-1 seeded), so every run
sees identical inputs.

\subsection{Models}
\textbf{MedGemma-4B} (\texttt{google/medgemma-4b-it}) is an open medical VLM whose SigLIP-style
encoder~\cite{zhai2023siglip} and language model were further trained on medical data; its model card lists
SLAKE (split unstated) but not VQA-RAD or PathVQA among training sources. \textbf{Gemma-3-4B}
(\texttt{google/gemma-3-4b-it}) shares its architecture and size. The two differ in their whole post-training,
not only in medical data, so we compare \emph{checkpoints} and do not attribute differences to medical data
alone. Both run unquantized in bf16 on one 16\,GB GPU (quantization would perturb the probabilities we audit)
and receive byte-identical prompts: a fixed system line, the question, and ``Answer with only `yes' or `no'.''
or ``Answer with a single word or short phrase.''

\subsection{Probes}
\label{sec:probes}
Every question is posed with its image (\textbf{orig}) and with screened paraphrases (\textbf{para$_k$},
original image; \cref{sec:para}). Reliance is probed five ways, each differing from \emph{orig} only in the image
or the instruction:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
\item \textbf{Image removed} (\emph{noimg}): image tokens omitted, text identical; the reference probe of the
taxonomy~\cite{sadanandan2026consistent}.
\item \textbf{Wrong image} (\emph{shuf}): another image from the same dataset and modality, chosen by a hash of
the question ID.
\item \textbf{R1, black image}: a black image in the image slot, in format but without content.
\item \textbf{R2, ``unknown'' allowed}: image removed, and the instruction adds ``If this cannot be determined
without seeing the image, answer `unknown'.''
\item \textbf{R3, opposite-answer image}: another image of the same dataset and modality on which the
\emph{same} question has the opposite gold answer. A model that uses the image must change its answer. Partners
exist for 367 SLAKE yes/no questions (130 images), whose templated questions recur across images.
\end{itemize}
The first two belong to the pre-registered main run. R1--R3 were registered after it, with directional
hypotheses (H6: MedGemma's answers survive a black image more; H7: with ``unknown'' allowed MedGemma still
declines less; H8: MedGemma follows opposite-answer images more), and run afterwards.

\subsection{Measures}
\textbf{Yes/no answers} come from one forward pass:
$P(\text{yes})=\sigma(\mathrm{LSE}_{t\in Y}\,\ell_t-\mathrm{LSE}_{t\in N}\,\ell_t)$ over the single-token
variants of \emph{yes} and \emph{no}; the first-token mass $m=P(Y)+P(N)$ is logged as a format check.
\textbf{Open answers} use greedy decoding and token-F1$\,\ge0.5$ after normalization, with an opposite-term
guard (left/right, upper/lower, \etc never match). \textbf{Consistent}: the answer on the first two valid
paraphrases equals the \emph{orig} answer. \textbf{Reliant} under a probe: the probe answer differs from
\emph{orig}. The \textbf{quadrant} follows from (consistent, reliant). \textbf{Refusal}: $m<0.5$, \ie most
first-token mass is on neither \emph{yes} nor \emph{no}; free generation confirms these are requests for the
image (\cref{fig:teaser}a). \textbf{Image PMI} of an answer $\hat y$ is $\log p(\hat y\mid I,q)-\log p(\hat
y\mid\varnothing,q)$. \textbf{Chance correction}: Cohen's $\kappa$~\cite{cohen1960kappa} between \emph{orig} and
probe answers; the \emph{chance floor} of the \dang{} share is $P(\text{consistent})\cdot p_e$, where $p_e$ is
the agreement expected from the two answer distributions alone.

\subsection{Paraphrase construction and screening}
\label{sec:para}
Paraphrase consistency is meaningful only if a paraphrase cannot change the correct answer. Candidates come
from Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct~\cite{qwen2024qwen25} (greedy; five styles) and from two deterministic templates that copy
every content word (``Is there X?''$\to$``Is X present?''). A rule validator rejects changes to laterality,
negation and absence words, quantities, antonyms, imaging planes, question form, answer leakage, near-copies and
length. Two audit rounds accepted 81\% and 83\%, below the pre-specified 85\%, so we tightened the rules,
excluded a ``plain language'' style, and \textbf{judged every unique rule-valid (question, paraphrase) pair},
4,890 in total, against a written rubric (\cref{app:rubric}). The judge was an LLM (Claude); see
\cref{sec:limits}. 1,208 pairs were rejected, each with a recorded reason (\eg \emph{mass$\to$lesion}, \emph{is
enlarged$\to$can be enlarged}), and unjudged pairs are rejected by construction. 84\% of the primary-set
questions retain at least two valid paraphrases; quadrant analyses use those (1,012 questions, 600 images).

\subsection{Statistics and pre-registration}
Hypotheses, endpoints, tests and exclusions were frozen before the main run~\cite{nosek2018prereg}; every later
change is listed in \cref{app:dev}, and post-hoc analyses are labeled as such. Several questions share an image,
so all intervals are percentile 95\% CIs from a cluster bootstrap over images~\cite{field2007bootstrap}
($B=2000$) with two-sided bootstrap $p$-values. Endpoints (\cref{tab:tests}): \textbf{P1a--c} blind accuracy minus
the majority-answer prior per dataset and \textbf{P2} AUROC(image PMI) $-$ AUROC(confidence), one Holm
family~\cite{holm1979}; \textbf{P3} the paired difference in \dang{} share, MedGemma $-$ Gemma-3; and
\textbf{H6--H8}, a second Holm family. A finding is called robust only if its sign holds across a grid of F1
thresholds (0.3/0.5/0.8), paraphrase counts (1/2/3) and ``strong'' flips.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}
Both runs completed (18,896 calls per model, plus 3,535 per model for R1--R3). Our pipeline reproduces
MedGemma's published SLAKE score (token-F1 70.2\ci{67.5}{72.7} \vs 72.3 on the model card; Gemma-3: 45.1 \vs
40.2), and the yes/no format mass with the image is $\ge0.997$ in every dataset. MedGemma is the more accurate
model with the image (\cref{tab:acc}), by 18 points on SLAKE and 25 on VQA-RAD yes/no.

\subsection{The reference probe: MedGemma looks more consistent but blind}
\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig1_quadrants.png}
\caption{Quadrant composition of yes/no answers (test). Left: reliance probed by removing the image (the
reference definition). Right: by a wrong image of the same modality. Shares are raw; on yes/no questions they
include chance agreement (\cref{sec:chance}) and correct answers (\cref{sec:why}).}
\label{fig:quad}
\end{figure*}

Under image removal MedGemma's \dang{} share is 50.6/46.8/56.5\% (PathVQA/SLAKE/VQA-RAD) against
43.2/28.1/31.0\% for Gemma-3 (\cref{fig:quad}, left). The paired difference, \textbf{P3 $=+13.7$
points}\ci{10.0}{17.5} ($p<0.001$; 1,012 questions, 600 images), is positive in every dataset (PathVQA
+7.5\ci{2.6}{12.3}, SLAKE +18.6\ci{12.2}{24.9}, VQA-RAD +25.6\ci{14.7}{36.5}) and in every cell of the
sensitivity grid. MedGemma is also the more consistent model (paraphrase flip rate 6.8\% \vs 13.6\% on SLAKE).
Read at face value, the medical checkpoint is more often stable, confident and blind.

\subsection{In-format probes reverse the ranking}
\label{sec:reverse}
\Cref{fig:reversal} places all four probes on one scale, the share of answers that change. Image removal is the
only one under which Gemma-3 changes more ($-6.1$\ci{$-9.5$}{$-2.7$} points). The three in-format probes
all say the opposite.

\paragraph{Opposite-answer image (R3).} This is the most direct test: the question is unchanged and the image now
calls for the other answer. MedGemma follows the image on 72.8\%\ci{68.1}{77.0} of swaps and Gemma-3 on
24.8\%\ci{20.4}{29.3} (H8, +48.0 points), so MedGemma is right on the new image 86\% of the time and Gemma-3 61\%.
The gap holds for CT (75 \vs 26\%), MRI (57 \vs 26\%) and X-ray (81 \vs 8\%; \cref{fig:opp}) and when 40 PathVQA
and VQA-RAD swaps are added (69.8 \vs 24.8\%, exploratory).

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig6_opposite.png}
\caption{Probe R3: share of answers that change when the image is replaced by one on which the same question
has the opposite correct answer (SLAKE yes/no, test+validation; 95\% CIs by image).}
\label{fig:opp}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Black image (R1).} H6 predicted that MedGemma's answers would survive a black image more often; it
failed in the opposite direction. Gemma-3 keeps the answer it gave with the real image on 72.9\% of questions,
MedGemma on 52.6\%; chance-corrected, $\kappa=0.33$\ci{0.28}{0.39} \vs 0.11\ci{0.06}{0.17}. Under this probe
Gemma-3 is the more \dang{} model by 14.0 points\ci{9.4}{18.6}. The answers show why: on a black image
MedGemma's yes-rate drops from 58\% to 28\% (it reads an empty image as absent findings), while Gemma-3's rises
from 64\% to 84\%, tracking the question rather than the image.

\paragraph{Wrong image.} A random image of the same modality changes MedGemma's answer more often (+5.1
points\ci{1.7}{8.5}); the \dang{} share under this probe does not differ ($-0.7$\ci{$-4.4$}{3.2}). It is the
weakest probe, because a random partner often has the same correct answer: where the partner image carries the
same question, \emph{all 23} chest X-ray partners had the same answer (CT 58\%, MRI 60\%). This explains why the
modality ordering of the \dang{} share reverses between probes (\cref{fig:mod}): X-ray is the least \dang{}
modality under image removal (33.1\%) and the most under a wrong image (75.4\%). The two probes agree poorly
($\kappa$ between their reliance labels $-0.11$ to 0.23).

\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig2_modality.png}
\caption{\dang{} share by modality (SLAKE yes/no, test and validation pooled as pre-specified; 95\% CIs by
image). The modality ordering reverses between probes.}
\label{fig:mod}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Why image removal misranks}
\label{sec:why}
\paragraph{Refusal.} The pre-registered format check ($m\ge0.9$) failed in exactly one condition, image removed.
Free generation explains it: ``\emph{Please provide the picture. I need to see the image to determine if there
is a spinal cord present}'' (Gemma-3). Gemma-3 would rather refuse on 354 of the 1,206 questions and MedGemma on
219 (\cref{fig:abst}; 14/41/50\% \vs 10/26/27\% by dataset). On those questions the forced answer is mostly
\emph{no} and unrelated to the model's answer with the image ($\kappa=-0.01$ for Gemma-3, 0.04 for MedGemma), so
53--55\% of them count as ``image-reliant''. Allowed to say ``unknown'' (R2), MedGemma declines on 93.0\% and
Gemma-3 on 99.7\%. H7's direction holds ($-6.7$ points) and MedGemma keeps a small tendency to answer blind,
concentrated in PathVQA (12\% answered), but most of the forced-format difference of 11.2 points disappears.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig4_abstention.png}
\caption{Share of yes/no questions on which the model declines to answer when the image is removed ($m<0.5$;
95\% CIs by image). Top: the main run's instruction (``Answer with only yes or no''). Bottom: probe R2, whose
instruction allows ``unknown''.}
\label{fig:abst}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Agreement between prior and image.} Refusal is not the whole story: on the 436 questions where both
models answer without the image ($m\ge0.9$), P3 is still +8.0\ci{2.9}{13.3}. Here MedGemma's blind answers are
informative. It beats the majority-answer prior on PathVQA (P1a, +5.0; +11.9\ci{7.1}{16.6} among questions it
answers), and its no-image answers agree with its image answers beyond chance ($\kappa=0.21$ \vs 0.11 for Gemma-3,
each on the questions it answers). A model that looks at the image and whose prior predicts what the image shows gives the
same answer with and without it, and image removal scores that as blind. The correctness split shows that this is
what MedGemma's excess consists of (\cref{fig:p3}, bottom): \dang{}-and-correct is 39.2\% \vs 25.1\%
(+14.1\ci{11.1}{17.1}), while \dang{}-and-wrong, the cell that would mislead a user, is 11.3\% \vs 11.7\%
($-0.4$\ci{$-2.7$}{2.0}). R3 removes this case by construction, and there MedGemma follows the image. The P1
margin also argues against memorization: it appears on PathVQA and VQA-RAD, which the model card does not list
as training data, and not on SLAKE, which it does.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig5_p3.png}
\caption{The MedGemma $-$ Gemma-3 difference in \dang{} share under each probe and subset, and split by whether
the \dang{} answer is correct (paired; 95\% CIs by image).}
\label{fig:p3}
\end{figure}

\subsection{The chance floor}
\label{sec:chance}
An answer counts as image-independent whenever the no-image answer equals the with-image answer, which on yes/no
questions happens often by chance. On the P3 set MedGemma's answers are unchanged without the image 58.6\% of the
time against 49.1\% expected from its answer distributions alone (Gemma-3: 49.7\% \vs 45.7\%). Combined with
consistency this gives a \textbf{chance floor of 41.5\% (MedGemma) and 35.8\% (Gemma-3)}, against observed
\dang{} shares of 50.5\% and 36.8\%. About 6 of the 13.7 points of P3 are the difference in floors, partly because
MedGemma is more consistent (84.5\% \vs 78.4\%), a desirable property the metric counts against it. Corrected for
chance the image-removal effect remains, $\Delta\kappa=+0.112$\ci{0.044}{0.180}, but it is the size of a
consistency difference, not of a model that ignores images.

\subsection{Does image reliance flag wrong answers?}
\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig3_selective.png}
\caption{AUROC for ranking correct above incorrect yes/no answers (test, 95\% CIs): the model's confidence
\vs label-free image reliance under each probe.}
\label{fig:sel}
\end{figure}

If image-independent answers were the unreliable ones, image reliance could serve as a warning signal. Ranking
each yes/no answer by its image PMI separates correct from incorrect answers at chance (\cref{fig:sel}; AUROC
\textbf{0.513}\ci{0.473}{0.552} for MedGemma, 0.532 for Gemma-3), while the model's own confidence reaches 0.709
and 0.603 (P2: better by 0.197\ci{0.145}{0.250} and 0.071\ci{0.026}{0.116}). The wrong-image variant is no better
(0.524, 0.536). Whether a model leaned on the image does not tell us whether it was right.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}
\paragraph{What image removal measures.} Removing the image asks a model a question about an image that is not
there. Its answer depends on whether it will answer at all and on how good its priors are, and only then on
whether it would have used the image. In our pair these two factors point the same way: the general checkpoint
refuses more and has weaker priors, so it looks more image-reliant, while every probe that keeps an image in the
input finds the medical checkpoint more reliant, by up to 48 points. The original study's corroborating checks
(black image, random swaps) agreed with image removal on its chest X-ray models~\cite{sadanandan2026consistent};
on our models and data they do not. Agreement between probes therefore has to be checked for each comparison
rather than assumed, and a \dang{} share is underspecified without its probe.

\paragraph{Where the residual risk is.} MedGemma's extra \dang{} answers are correct, and the stable,
image-independent and wrong cell is the same for both models. The remaining concern is that MedGemma's errors,
fewer overall (25.7\% \vs 37.6\%), are more often of this kind (44\% \vs 31\%, +12.9\ci{6.0}{19.9}), so a
consistency or reliance check would miss them. It also answers without an image on 7\% of questions even when
allowed to decline.

\paragraph{Recommendations for reliance audits.} (1)~Probe reliance in format, ideally with an image that calls
for a different answer, and report agreement between probes. (2)~Report the \dang{} share with its chance floor or
as $\kappa$; on balanced yes/no data a model whose blind answers are pure noise is about 50\% ``not reliant''.
(3)~Split \dang{} by correctness. (4)~Allow abstention, and treat declining without an image as desirable rather
than as a format failure.

\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limits}
One model pair shows that image removal \emph{can} misrank models, not how often it does; more pairs are needed,
and the two checkpoints differ in their whole post-training, not only in medical data. The probes were registered
after the main results were known (before running them), and one of three predictions failed. R3 is limited to
SLAKE, where questions recur across images. SLAKE is in MedGemma's training data (split unstated). Refusal is
inferred from first-token mass and confirmed on a sample by free generation, not annotated per question.
Paraphrase equivalence was judged by an LLM and \textbf{was not validated by human raters}; this is the main
limitation of the consistency measure, and an LLM judge may share blind spots with the paraphraser. PathVQA
questions are auto-generated and often ungrammatical. The correctness split, the chance correction and the
refusal split were added after seeing the results. All 330 pilot questions used to tune the design are inside the
evaluation set; excluding them leaves every conclusion unchanged (P1a +6.3\ci{2.4}{10.6}, P3 +12.9\ci{8.9}{17.1}).
Benchmark VQA is not clinical use, and nothing here is a clinical claim.

\section{Implementation Details}
\label{sec:impl}
\paragraph{Pipeline.} A Python package (\texttt{medvlm}) with a command-line interface: \texttt{prepare}
(download, deterministic sampling, SHA-checked images), \texttt{paraphrase} (generation plus rule and judgment
validation, fail-closed), \texttt{pipeline} (resumable inference in parts with checkpoint analysis),
\texttt{probes} (R1--R3), \texttt{analyze}, \texttt{compare} and \texttt{posthoc} (all tables and figures here).
Configs layer base, profile, model and hardware settings. Each job is one (question, condition) pair keyed by ID,
so interrupted runs resume without recomputation, and every run records its config, commit and library versions.

\paragraph{Inference.} PyTorch 2.11 and Hugging Face Transformers 5.19, bf16, SDPA attention, one RTX 4080 SUPER
(16\,GB). A full run is 18,896 calls per model at 0.23\,s per call (about 75 minutes, 8.2\,GB peak). During
pre-flight we found that in bf16 the \emph{batch size} changes teacher-forced log-probabilities by up to 1.09 nats
(median 0.17) even with identical, unpadded inputs, while $P(\text{yes})$ changes by at most 0.008. An fp32 output
head did not remove it, so the cause is inside the network. All runs therefore use batch size 1, which costs about
1.5$\times$ throughput. A regression check reproduced the T4 pilot on the new GPU (98.5\% identical answers, mean
$|\Delta P(\text{yes})|=0.004$).

\paragraph{Testing.} 96 unit tests and 7 real-model tests cover, among others, scoring edge cases, paraphrase
rules (including each failure class found in the audit), batching equivalence, crash-safe resume, the coverage
of the clustered bootstrap (by simulation), the test-split restriction of P3, chance agreement of $\kappa$, and
the construction of opposite-answer partners.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}
Is a small medical VLM consistent but blind? By the image-removal test it looks that way, more than its
general-purpose twin. By every test that keeps an image in the input it is the opposite: the medical checkpoint
follows the image more, by up to 48 points. Image removal measures whether a model answers without an image and
whether its priors agree with the image, and both differ between the two checkpoints. Reliance audits that compare
models need in-format probes, chance correction and a correctness split.

\appendix
\section{Paraphrase equivalence rubric}
\label{app:rubric}
A pair is \textbf{accepted} only if it asks exactly the same thing, so the correct answer cannot differ.
Allowed: perception framing (``can X be seen'', ``is X visible'', ``can X be seen to be enlarged''), exact
synonyms (clavicle/collarbone, encephalon/brain, intravenous contrast/dye), reordering. \textbf{Rejected}: a
fact turned into a possibility or capability (``Is the heart enlarged?''$\to$``Can the heart be enlarged?'');
a broadened or narrowed term (mass$\to$lesion, organs$\to$structures, digestive system$\to$GI tract, skull
fracture$\to$cranial injury); a changed scope or presupposition (``Do the organs exist in X''$\to$``Are there
organs in X''); added qualifiers, findings or modality (``bilaterally'', ``on imaging studies'',
``radiograph''); a reversed or changed relation (``does A show B''$\to$``is A associated with B'', ``mass
lateral to X''$\to$``X lateral to mass''); antonyms (healthy$\leftrightarrow$unhealthy,
coronal$\to$transverse); two questions in one; malformed text. Rejections by class: relation 447, term 364,
modal 106, added content 102, organ$\to$structure 47, generic collapse 30, polarity 19, scope 9 (plus
template-pass rejections).
